source: https://rbi.org.in/Scripts/HolidayMatrixDisplay.aspx
text: RBI Bank Holidays — How Bank Holidays Are Determined RBI publishes a Bank Holiday matrix, filterable by RBI regional office (covering all major cities from Agartala to Vijayawada), month, and year, showing when banks in that region will be closed. Two Categories of Closure: 1. Negotiable Instruments Act (NI Act) Holidays — statutory closures declared under the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881. These are public holidays on which cheques/negotiable instruments cannot be presented, and banks are closed. 2. Banks' Closing of Accounts — additional closure periods relating to half-yearly/annual account-closing activity, distinct from NI Act holidays. General Rule: All scheduled and non-scheduled banks observe a public holiday on the second and fourth Saturday of every month, in addition to the region-specific NI Act holidays (which vary by state/region — e.g. a regional festival observed as a bank holiday in one RBI regional office's jurisdiction may not be a holiday elsewhere in the country). How To Use This For A Specific Date: The actual list of holiday dates is region- and year-specific and changes annually — this document intentionally does NOT reproduce a dated list, since it would go stale immediately. For a specific date, region, and year, check RBI's live Holiday Matrix directly, filtering by the relevant RBI regional office. This matters for banking staff/customers when planning cheque clearing, RTGS/NEFT cut-offs, or any date-sensitive transaction around a potential regional holiday.

source: shabdavali.rbi.org.in (RBI's official banking glossary — page itself is CAPTCHA-gated and could not be scraped directly; terms below are standard, well-established RBI/banking terminology cross-checked against multiple financial-education sources, not copied from the RBI page itself)
text: RBI Banking Glossary — Common Terms Repo Rate: The rate at which RBI lends short-term funds (typically overnight) to commercial banks against government securities. RBI's primary tool for controlling inflation and short-term liquidity. Reverse Repo Rate: The rate at which RBI borrows funds from commercial banks, absorbing excess liquidity from the banking system. Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR): The percentage of a bank's total deposits that it must keep as reserves with RBI (in cash, not lent out or invested). Ensures banks retain enough liquidity to meet withdrawal demand. Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR): The percentage of a bank's net demand and time liabilities that must be held in specified liquid assets (cash, gold, approved government securities). A separate reserve requirement from CRR, also set by RBI. Non-Performing Asset (NPA): A loan or advance where the borrower has not paid interest or principal for a specified period (generally 90 days) — classified as NPA rather than a performing/standard asset, directly affecting a bank's reported asset quality and profitability. Marginal Cost of Funds based Lending Rate (MCLR): An internal benchmark rate a bank uses to price loans, based on its marginal (incremental) cost of raising funds; many older/legacy loans are still priced as a spread over MCLR (see sbi_rates_lending_structured for an example of MCLR-linked loan pricing). External Benchmark Rate (EBR/EBLR): A lending benchmark tied directly to an external, RBI-published rate (usually the repo rate) rather than a bank's own internal cost of funds — used for most new retail and MSME loans since RBI mandated external benchmarking for these segments. Bank Rate: The rate at which RBI is ready to buy or rediscount bills of exchange or other eligible commercial paper — a longer-standing, less frequently used policy tool than the repo rate. Marginal Standing Facility (MSF) Rate: The rate at which banks can borrow overnight funds from RBI against government securities, beyond what is available under the standard repo window — typically priced above the repo rate as a penal/emergency-liquidity rate. This is a general reference glossary, not a substitute for RBI's own Master Circulars/Directions on any given topic — always confirm the precise regulatory definition of a term against the specific Direction/Circular it comes from before citing it as binding.

source: https://rbi.org.in/Scripts/CitiChart.aspx
text: RBI Citizen's Charter — Service Delivery Commitments RBI's Citizen's Charter lists roughly 213 distinct services across 9 RBI departments, each with a committed processing timeline. Departments Covered: - Currency Management — currency chest applications, note exchange. - Government & Bank Accounts — challans, drafts, cash transactions, refinancing. - Payment Systems — certificate authorisation, membership applications. - Regulation — licensing/approvals for banks, NBFCs, Asset Reconstruction Companies (ARCs), and other financial institutions. - Supervision — statutory auditor appointment approvals. - Enforcement — compounding of contraventions (regulatory violations). - Financial Markets — benchmark administration, trading platform authorisation. - Foreign Exchange — Authorised Dealer (AD) authorisations, External Commercial Borrowing (ECB) approvals, investment transaction approvals. - Internal Debt Management — primary dealer licensing, government securities account services. Service Timelines: Committed processing windows range from as short as 3 days to as long as 270 days, with most falling between 15 and 90 calendar days. The timeline clock starts only once RBI has received a complete application (all required documents/information submitted) — incomplete submissions do not start the countdown. Application Channel: Most applications for RBI services under this Charter are submitted through the PRAVAAH platform (RBI's centralised regulatory application portal). This is a general service-standard reference — the exact timeline for a specific service should be checked against the current published Charter, since individual service timelines can be revised.

source: https://rbi.org.in/Scripts/Complaints.aspx
text: RBI Complaint Process — How To File a Complaint Two Distinct Complaint Channels: 1. Complaint AGAINST a Regulated Entity (bank, NBFC, or System Participant): File online through RBI's Complaint Management System (CMS) at cms.rbi.org.in. This is the correct channel for a customer's grievance against their own bank or any other RBI-regulated entity (deficient service, unresolved dispute, etc.) — this is also the intake point that feeds into the Reserve Bank - Integrated Ombudsman Scheme (RB-IOS) process (see rbi_grievance_ombudsman_2026 for the substantive scheme rules — no monetary cap, escalation timelines, etc.). 2. Complaint AGAINST RBI Itself: For a grievance about an RBI department directly (not about a bank or other regulated entity), email crpc@rbi.org.in with: name, address, the specific RBI department concerned, and supporting documents. Key Distinction To Get Right: A customer complaint about their OWN BANK's service should go through CMS (cms.rbi.org.in) and, if unresolved, escalates under the Ombudsman Scheme — NOT to crpc@rbi.org.in, which is only for complaints about RBI's own departments/conduct. This is a process/channel reference — the substantive rules for what qualifies, escalation timelines, and monetary limits are covered separately in the Ombudsman Scheme documents, not repeated here.

source: Cross-checked across multiple financial data aggregators citing RBI Monetary Policy; verify against rbi.org.in before treating as final
text: RBI Current Policy Rates As of the last confirmed change (5 December 2025), RBI's key policy rates are: Repo Rate: 5.25% p.a. Reverse Repo Rate: 3.35% p.a. Marginal Standing Facility (MSF) Rate: 5.50% p.a. Bank Rate: 5.50% p.a. Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR): 3.00% Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR): 18.00% IMPORTANT: This category (RBI_CURRENT_RATES) is explicitly flagged in the system prompt as volatile — these rates change at RBI's bi-monthly Monetary Policy Committee reviews (and occasionally between reviews). This document reflects the rate as of the DATE above, not necessarily today's rate. Always verify the current figure on rbi.org.in or via RBI's official Monetary Policy Statement before quoting it as current. This is the clearest example in the whole pool of why a static file needs a refresh cadence rather than being treated as permanently correct.

source: https://www.dicgc.org.in/guide-to-deposit-insurance
text: Deposit Insurance in India (DICGC) Bank deposits in India are insured by the Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation (DICGC), a wholly owned subsidiary of the Reserve Bank of India, established under the DICGC Act, 1961. Each depositor in a bank is insured up to a maximum of Rs. 5,00,000 (Rupees Five Lakh) for both principal and interest amount held by them, across all their deposits in that bank, taken together. This limit covers savings, fixed, current, and recurring deposit accounts. This insurance is automatic and free to the depositor — banks pay the premium to DICGC, not the customer. No application or opt-in is required. Coverage applies per bank, not per branch — deposits held in the same capacity and same right across all branches of one bank are added together and insured up to the Rs. 5,00,000 limit as a whole, not per branch. Nearly all commercial banks operating in India, including foreign bank branches, local area banks, regional rural banks, and cooperative banks, are covered by DICGC insurance. This limit is set by DICGC/RBI and is subject to revision by the government from time to time — always confirm the current limit on dicgc.org.in or rbi.org.in before stating it as final.

source: https://www.business-standard.com/finance/news/central-state-co-op-banks-brought-under-ambit-of-rbi-s-ombudsman-scheme-125100701358_1.html
text: RBI Grievance Redressal — Reserve Bank - Integrated Ombudsman Scheme, 2021 (RB-IOS 2021) [SUPERSEDED] NOTE: This scheme was replaced by RB-IOS 2026, effective 1 July 2026. This document is kept only as historical/reference context — do not present this as the current scheme. RB-IOS 2021 was launched in November 2021, unifying three earlier RBI ombudsman schemes into a single "One Nation, One Ombudsman" framework. It provided a cost-free, expeditious grievance redress mechanism for customers of RBI-regulated entities. In October 2025, coverage was extended to state and central co-operative banks, and non-scheduled primary (urban) co-operative banks with deposits of Rs. 50 crore or more, alongside existing coverage of commercial banks, regional rural banks, and most NBFCs. Under RB-IOS 2021, the scheme had different (lower) compensation limits and procedural rules than the current 2026 version — for exact current figures, refer to the RB-IOS 2026 document, not this one.

source: https://www.rbi.org.in/commonman/Upload/English/FAQs/PDFs/RBIOS01072026.pdf
text: RBI Grievance Redressal — Reserve Bank - Integrated Ombudsman Scheme, 2026 (RB-IOS 2026) RB-IOS 2026 came into force on 1 July 2026 (issued 16 January 2026), replacing the Reserve Bank - Integrated Ombudsman Scheme, 2021 (RB-IOS 2021). This is the current scheme in effect. If a customer has a complaint about deficiency in service by a bank or other RBI-regulated entity, and it is not resolved to their satisfaction or not replied to within the applicable time limit, they can escalate it under RB-IOS 2026. Key points of the current scheme: - No monetary limit on the amount in dispute that can be brought before the RBI Ombudsman. - The RBI Ombudsman can award compensation up to Rs. 30 lakh for consequential loss, plus up to Rs. 3 lakh separately for the complainant's time, expenses, and mental anguish/harassment. - Complaints can be filed online via the Complaint Management System at cms.rbi.org.in, or by email/physical mode. - Coverage includes all Commercial Banks, Regional Rural Banks, State and Central Co-operative Banks (subject to deposit-size thresholds), NBFCs, payment system operators, and Credit Information Companies. - A Regulated Entity or a complainant can appeal an Ombudsman's Award to the Appellate Authority within 30 days of receiving it. - Complaints received before 1 July 2026, and appeals/execution of earlier Awards, continue to be governed by the older RB-IOS 2021 rules. Within the bank, the Principal Nodal Officer (typically a General Manager-level official) represents the bank and provides information for complaints filed against it. This scheme replaced RB-IOS 2021 — if you encounter older material citing the 2021 scheme's monetary caps or procedures, treat this 2026 version as current and the 2021 material as superseded.

source: https://www.rbi.org.in/scripts/deputygovernors.aspx and RBI press release, 11 December 2024 (Governor appointment)
text: RBI Leadership — Governor and Deputy Governors Governor: Shri Sanjay Malhotra took charge as Governor of the Reserve Bank of India on 11 December 2024, appointed for a 3-year term. He is the 26th Governor of RBI (the 15th to come from the civil services), and succeeded Shaktikanta Das, who completed a 6-year term. Sanjay Malhotra is a 1990-batch IAS officer of the Rajasthan cadre, and was Revenue Secretary in the Ministry of Finance immediately before this appointment. Deputy Governors (as listed on RBI's official Deputy Governors page, current as of the dates below): - Shri Rohit Jain — took charge 4 May 2026. - Shri Shirish Chandra Murmu — took charge 9 October 2025. - Dr. Poonam Gupta — took charge 2 May 2025. - Shri Swaminathan J — RBI's page listed his term as extending to 25 June 2026 at last check. IMPORTANT — verify before quoting: Deputy Governor terms are fixed and this is exactly the kind of fact that goes stale. Shri Swaminathan J's listed term end-date (25 June 2026) may already have passed depending on today's date — there may be a new 4th Deputy Governor not reflected here. Always cross-check the live list at rbi.org.in/scripts/deputygovernors.aspx before stating who currently holds all four Deputy Governor posts. This is general organizational information about RBI, not a regulatory rule or rate — kept in the RBI pool because bank staff may need this for correspondence, citations, or context, not because it is itself a directive.

source: RBI Master Direction (Commercial Banks - Asset Classification, Provisioning and Income Recognition) Directions, 2026, issued 27 April 2026, effective 1 April 2027 — SUPERSEDES the earlier (Commercial Banks - Income Recognition, Asset Classification and Provisioning) Directions, 2025 issued 28 November 2025; catalog PDFs: rbidocs.rbi.org.in/rdocs/notification/PDFs/MD39857992A3DBE7946619F0F76DF81E472CF.PDF (2026) and .../164MD.PDF (2025) — both CAPTCHA-gated for direct fetch; content below is cross-checked from multiple regulatory-tracking sources; verify against the primary Direction before treating as legally binding
text: RBI Master Direction — Asset Classification, Provisioning and Income Recognition (Commercial Banks) IMPORTANT — Two directions exist on this same topic, in force at different times: 1. The 2025 Direction (issued 28 November 2025) — the current applicable rules until the 2026 version takes effect. 2. The 2026 Direction (issued 27 April 2026) — comes into force only from 1 April 2027. Until then, the 2025 Direction's NPA classification rules remain the operative standard. 2025 Direction — Core Rules (currently in force): Defines NPA categories (Substandard, Doubtful, Loss assets), security valuation norms, and "out-of-order" criteria for overdraft/cash-credit facilities used to determine NPA status. Interest income is recognised on an accrual basis only for standard (performing) assets; NPAs must be recognised on a cash basis only (income is booked only when actually received). All accounts must be covered under an automated, IT-based system for classification, upgradation, and provisioning — classification as overdue, SMA (Special Mention Account), or NPA, and any upgradation, must happen automatically as part of the bank's day-end processing, not via manual/discretionary flagging. 2026 Direction — What Changes From 1 April 2027: Introduces a staging framework for asset classification under an Expected Credit Loss (ECL) approach — a forward-looking provisioning model — while RETAINING the existing NPA classification norms alongside it. This is a significant methodology shift (from purely incurred-loss provisioning to a forward-looking ECL model), so banking staff should be aware a transition is coming, even though it isn't live yet. When answering a question about "current" asset classification rules, default to the 2025 Direction unless the question specifically asks about the post-April-2027 ECL framework.

source: RBI Master Direction (Commercial Banks - Branch Authorisation) Directions, 2025, issued 28 November 2025; catalog PDF: rbidocs.rbi.org.in/rdocs/notification/PDFs/147MD.PDF (CAPTCHA-gated for direct fetch — content below is cross-checked from multiple regulatory-tracking sources reporting the official text; verify against the primary Direction before treating as legally binding)
text: RBI Master Direction — Branch Authorisation (Commercial Banks) Consolidates rules on opening, shifting, merging, and closing banking outlets and related off-site units (ATMs, Business Correspondent points, Doorstep Banking arrangements). Applies to all commercial banks except Small Finance Banks, Payments Banks, and Local Area Banks. In force with immediate effect from 28 November 2025. Board Responsibility: Banks' Boards must adopt a board-approved policy for branch-network decisions, and for Digital Banking Units (DBUs), Business Correspondents (BCs), Mobile/Off-site ATMs, and Doorstep Banking — with clearly assigned oversight duties, not left to branch-level discretion. Opening Outlets WITHOUT Prior RBI Permission: Scheduled commercial banks may open new banking outlets without RBI's prior permission, PROVIDED at least 25% of the outlets opened in a period are in Unbanked Rural Centres (URCs) — including rural, Left-Wing-Extremism (LWE) affected districts, or North-Eastern states. Opening MORE than the required 25% in a given period earns a carried- forward credit usable for up to 2 subsequent years. When Prior RBI Approval IS Required: - Opening at sensitive locations (as defined by RBI/security considerations). - Branches conducting government business. - Any bank whose general branch-opening permission has been withdrawn by RBI. Such requests go through the PRAVAAH portal and, once granted, remain valid for one year. Minimum Service Standards: The Direction also prescribes minimum service standards for fixed- point service delivery at a banking outlet (not detailed further here — check the primary Direction for the specific standards).

source: RBI Master Direction (Commercial Banks - Prudential Norms on Capital Adequacy) Directions, 2025, issued 28 November 2025 (updated as on 18 May 2026); catalog PDF: rbidocs.rbi.org.in/rdocs/notification/PDFs/151MD.PDF (CAPTCHA-gated for direct fetch — content below is cross-checked from multiple regulatory-tracking sources covering this and closely related AIFI/RRB Directions issued the same framework; verify the commercial-bank-specific figures against the primary Direction before treating as legally binding)
text: RBI Master Direction — Prudential Norms on Capital Adequacy (Commercial Banks) Minimum CRAR (Capital to Risk-weighted Assets Ratio): 9% of risk-weighted assets at all times — the baseline requirement before adding the capital conservation buffer below. Capital Conservation Buffer (CCB): An additional 2.5% is required on top of the base 9% CRAR, making the effective minimum CRAR requirement 11.5% in practice. Tier 1 / Tier 2 Composition (per RBI's parallel Direction for All India Financial Institutions, which follows the same broad framework — confirm the exact commercial-bank split against the primary Direction): - Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1): minimum around 5.5% of risk-weighted assets. - Total Tier 1 capital: minimum around 7%. - Tier 2 capital: capped at a maximum of 100% of total Tier 1 capital for capital-adequacy compliance purposes. Why This Matters Operationally: CRAR is the headline solvency metric RBI and the public use to judge a bank's financial strength — falling below the effective 11.5% threshold (base + buffer) can trigger supervisory action (see RBI's Prompt Corrective Action framework, a separate mechanism not detailed here). Given related Directions exist for RRBs, AIFIs, and NBFCs with different specific percentages, always confirm which entity-type Direction applies before quoting a CRAR figure for a non-commercial-bank entity.

source: RBI Master Direction (Commercial Banks - Credit Cards and Debit Cards: Issuance and Conduct) Directions, 2025, issued 28 November 2025; catalog PDF: rbidocs.rbi.org.in/rdocs/notification/PDFs/155MD.PDF (CAPTCHA-gated for direct fetch — content below is cross-checked from multiple regulatory-tracking sources reporting the official text; verify against the primary Direction before treating as legally binding)
text: RBI Master Direction — Credit Cards and Debit Cards: Issuance and Conduct (Commercial Banks) Applies immediately to all commercial banks, including SBI and other new banks (a consolidation of prior circulars into a single Direction). Board-Approved Policy Required, Covering: Interest rates, fees, credit limits, customer consent procedures, grievance redressal, and co-branding arrangements (co-branded cards issued jointly with a non-bank partner). Consent and Issuance Rules: - Explicit customer consent is required before issuing a card. - Unsolicited or unilateral credit-limit upgrades are prohibited — a bank cannot raise a customer's limit without the customer's agreement. - Charges and Annual Percentage Rate (APR) must be clearly disclosed upfront, not buried in fine print. Billing, Refunds, and Reviews: Strict adherence to billing-cycle and refund-processing procedures is required. Card-issuers must review their card operations semi-annually through their Audit Committee, actively monitor credit risk on the card portfolio, and ensure EMI-conversion offers on card spends are transparent (clear disclosure of the effective interest rate, not just the EMI amount). This Direction is the regulatory basis for card-related customer protections — e.g. why a bank cannot silently raise a credit limit, or must clearly disclose the APR on a card before issuance.

source: RBI Master Direction (Commercial Banks - Credit Risk Management) Directions, 2025 (and Amendment/Second Amendment Directions, 2025-2026); catalog PDF: rbidocs.rbi.org.in/rdocs/notification/PDFs/157MD.PDF (CAPTCHA-gated for direct fetch — content below is cross-checked from multiple regulatory-tracking sources reporting the official text; verify against the primary Direction before treating as legally binding. Note: this is a DIFFERENT Direction from "Concentration Risk Management" — the two are easily confused since both concern credit exposure risk, but Concentration Risk Management specifically governs large/connected-counterparty exposure limits, while this Direction covers the broader credit risk framework)
text: RBI Master Direction — Credit Risk Management (Commercial Banks) Applies to commercial banking companies (excluding Small Finance Banks, Payments Banks, Local Area Banks), corresponding new banks, and SBI. Related-Party Lending Restrictions: Restricts loans to a bank's own directors, their relatives, and reciprocal lending arrangements (bank A lending to bank B's director in exchange for bank B lending to bank A's director) — such loans require specific Board approval and are not routine credit decisions. Legal Entity Identifier (LEI) Requirement: Non-individual borrowers with aggregate exposure of Rs. 5 crore or more must obtain and keep renewing an LEI code — intended to improve transparency and data accuracy on who a bank is actually exposed to across the financial system. CEO / Whole-Time Director Loans: Loans and advances to a bank's own CEO or Whole-Time Directors require approval by the Board of Directors, a Board committee with delegated powers, or the Appointments Committee — not ordinary credit-approval channels. Unhedged Foreign Currency Exposure (UFCE): Banks must assess UFCE risk in borrowers (i.e. borrowers with foreign- currency-denominated debt or income exposure without hedging), since exchange-rate volatility can impair a borrower's repayment capacity. Where UFCE risk is material, banks must apply incremental provisioning and capital charges reflecting potential losses, and should encourage borrowers to hedge. This Direction sets the credit-risk-management framework banks must have in place — it's a governance/process requirement more than a single numeric threshold, unlike Capital Adequacy or CRR/SLR.

source: RBI Master Direction (Commercial Banks - Cash Reserve Ratio and Statutory Liquidity Ratio) Directions, 2025, issued 28 November 2025; catalog PDF: rbidocs.rbi.org.in/rdocs/notification/PDFs/150MD.PDF (CAPTCHA-gated for direct fetch — content below is cross-checked from multiple regulatory-tracking sources reporting the official text; verify against the primary Direction before treating as legally binding)
text: RBI Master Direction — Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) and Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR), Commercial Banks Consolidates all commercial-bank reserve-requirement rules into a single Direction, issued 28 November 2025. CRR Phased Schedule (as of the 2025 Directions): A phased reduction was scheduled: 3.75% -> 3.5% -> 3.25% -> 3.00% of Net Demand and Time Liabilities (NDTL), effective from the reporting fortnights beginning 6 September, 4 October, 1 November, and 29 November 2025 respectively. Current CRR: 3.00% (consistent with the rate confirmed in rbi_current_policy_rates for December 2025). SLR Requirement: Minimum 18.00% of NDTL, held in specified liquid assets (cash, approved government securities, gold). Minimum Daily CRR Maintenance: Banks must maintain at least 90% of the prescribed average CRR on any given day within the reporting fortnight (not just meet the average over the full period). NDTL Computation Notes: The Direction clarifies treatment of inter-bank items, foreign currency deposits, and Upper Tier II instruments, and lists specific exclusions from NDTL (paid-up capital, certain refinance amounts, tax provisions, specified government/agency receipts). Since CRR/SLR are reviewed at RBI's bi-monthly Monetary Policy Committee meetings (same cadence as the repo rate — see rbi_current_policy_rates), always confirm the currently-effective percentage before quoting it as final.

source: RBI Master Direction (Commercial Banks - Digital Banking Channels Authorisation) Directions, 2025, issued 28 November 2025, effective 1 January 2026; catalog PDF: rbidocs.rbi.org.in/rdocs/notification/PDFs/380MD.PDF (CAPTCHA-gated for direct fetch — content below is cross-checked from multiple regulatory-tracking sources reporting the official text; verify against the primary Direction before treating as legally binding)
text: RBI Master Direction — Digital Banking Channels Authorisation (Commercial Banks) Issued 28 November 2025, effective from 1 January 2026 — a consolidated regulatory framework for how commercial banks are allowed to launch and operate digital banking services. Scope: applies to commercial banking companies (excluding Small Finance Banks, Payments Banks, Local Area Banks), corresponding new banks, and SBI, as defined under the Banking Regulation Act, 1949. Channels Covered: Internet banking, mobile banking apps, USSD (Unstructured Supplementary Service Data — e.g. the *99# banking service), SMS-based banking, and other electronic platforms. The Direction distinguishes View-Only facilities (balance/statement checking only) from Transactional facilities (actual fund transfers/payments). Approval Requirement: Prior RBI approval is required specifically before launching a TRANSACTIONAL digital banking facility (not for view-only facilities). Banks apply to their Regional Office of RBI through the PRAVAAH portal, subject to meeting prudential eligibility criteria, and must submit a Board resolution plus supporting documents alongside the application. This is the regulatory basis for why launching a new transactional mobile/internet banking feature requires RBI sign-off, while a read-only balance-check feature generally does not.

source: RBI Master Direction (Commercial Banks - Governance) Directions, 2025, issued 28 November 2025; catalog PDF: rbidocs.rbi.org.in/rdocs/notification/PDFs/149MD.PDF (CAPTCHA-gated for direct fetch — content below is cross-checked from multiple regulatory-tracking sources reporting the official text; verify against the primary Direction before treating as legally binding)
text: RBI Master Direction — Governance (Commercial Banks) Board Committee Structure: - Audit Committee of the Board (ACB): must comprise only Non-Executive Directors, with financial expertise required among members. - Risk Management Committee of the Board (RMCB): must have a majority of Non-Executive Directors. - Nomination and Remuneration Committee (NRC): handles director appointments and compensation policy. Fit-and-Proper Director Criteria: - Age: 35-67 years for Public Sector Banks (PSBs); up to 75 years for Private Banks (PVBs) — a materially different upper limit between the two. - Minimum qualification: a graduate degree, plus expertise in banking, finance, law, IT, risk management, or agriculture. - Disqualifications include holding a political position, involvement in para-banking activities, or a conflict of interest. Board's Strategic Focus Areas (7 themes RBI expects boards to prioritise): 1. Business Strategy — product innovation, competitiveness. 2. Risk Management — credit, market, liquidity risk policy oversight. 3. Financial Integrity — scrutiny of NPAs and provisioning adequacy. 4. Compliance — adherence to RBI and SEBI norms. 5. Customer Protection — preventing mis-selling, grievance resolution. 6. Financial Inclusion — priority sector lending, microfinance. 7. Human Resources — training, incentive structures, internal governance of staff. This Direction governs how a bank's own Board must be structured and what it must actively oversee — relevant context for understanding why a bank's decision-making process looks the way it does, not a customer-facing rule.

source: RBI Master Direction (Reserve Bank of India - Interest Rate on Advances) Directions, 2016, updated 1 October 2025; catalog PDF: rbidocs.rbi.org.in/rdocs/notification/PDFs/161MD.PDF (CAPTCHA-gated for direct fetch — content below is cross-checked from multiple regulatory-tracking sources reporting the official text; verify against the primary Direction before treating as legally binding)
text: RBI Master Direction — Interest Rates on Advances (Commercial Banks) Originally issued in 2016, most recently updated 1 October 2025. Benchmark Framework: Banks must price rupee advances (subject to specified exemptions) by reference to an internal benchmark (Marginal Cost of Funds based Lending Rate, MCLR) or an External Benchmark Lending Rate (EBLR, typically tied to the repo rate), plus a Board-approved, bank-defined spread — negotiating outside this framework is not permitted. MCLR Composition: Marginal cost of funds + negative carry on CRR + operating costs + a tenor premium. MCLR is tenor-linked (published at specified maturities) and reviewed monthly, or quarterly where permitted. Reset Periodicity: For floating-rate loans, the periodicity of interest-rate reset must be one year or less, and the exact periodicity must be stated in the loan contract itself — a bank cannot leave this open-ended or apply an undisclosed reset schedule. EBLR Adoption Trend (market context, not a rule): As of December 2024, roughly 61% of total floating-rate loans were linked to an external benchmark (EBLR), versus about 36% still on MCLR — RBI has been steering the system toward external benchmarking for better monetary-policy transmission. This governs how ANY commercial bank must structure its lending rates — it's the regulatory basis behind why a bank's home/personal/vehicle loan rate resets when RBI changes the repo rate.

source: RBI Master Direction (Reserve Bank of India - Interest Rate on Deposits) Directions, 2025 (RBI/2025-26/134), effective 1 April 2025; catalog PDF: rbidocs.rbi.org.in/rdocs/notification/PDFs/153MD.PDF (CAPTCHA-gated for direct fetch — content below is cross-checked from multiple regulatory-tracking sources reporting the official text; verify against the primary Direction before treating as legally binding)
text: RBI Master Direction — Interest Rate on Deposits (Commercial Banks) Consolidates and replaces the previous 2016-era Master Directions on deposit interest rates, effective 1 April 2025, applicable to all banks in India (not commercial banks alone). Premature Withdrawal: - Banks may choose to offer term deposits WITHOUT a premature withdrawal option, EXCEPT that all term deposits from individuals (singly or jointly held) of Rs. 1 crore and below MUST carry a premature withdrawal facility — this is a floor protection for retail depositors, not optional for the bank. - A prematurely withdrawn deposit earns interest at the rate applicable to the amount/period actually held, NOT the originally contracted rate for the full tenor. - No interest at all is payable if premature withdrawal happens before completing the minimum period of 7 days. Senior Citizens / Retired Staff: Banks may offer additional interest to specified categories including senior citizens and retired staff — this is permitted, not a fixed mandated premium (compare to the specific rate a given bank actually publishes, e.g. sbi_rates_deposit_structured, indianbank rates). General Rules Banks Must Follow: - Must adopt a Board-approved policy covering the interest-rate schedule, premature-withdrawal penalties, and specific rules for NRE/NRO/FCNR(B) deposits. - Interest rates must be UNIFORM across all branches and customers for comparable deposits accepted on the same date — negotiating an individual customer's rate is prohibited. This is the regulatory floor/framework — an individual bank's actual published rates (e.g. SBI's or Indian Bank's FD tables) must comply with this Direction but are set by the bank itself within it.

text: RBI Master Direction — Know Your Customer (KYC), Commercial Banks Issued 28 November 2025 as one of RBI's sector-specific KYC Directions (10 institution types covered, including commercial banks, NBFCs, payments banks, and cooperative banks, each under its own Direction). Risk Categorisation: Customers must be categorised as Low, Medium, or High risk based on identity, business/occupation, geography, and transaction-type factors. Periodic KYC Update Frequency (by risk category): - High-risk customers: full KYC updation at least once every 2 years. - Medium-risk customers: once every 8 years. - Low-risk customers: once every 10 years. June 2025 Amendment: The Reserve Bank of India (KYC) (Amendment) Directions, 2025 (effective immediately from 12 June 2025) gave low-risk individual customers extra time to complete a due periodic KYC update — up to one year after the due date, or up to 30 June 2026, whichever is later. This is a binding regulatory rule, not guidance — banks are required to enforce these periodicities, not merely recommend them to customers. Given the amendment history, always check whether a further amendment has superseded these specific timelines before treating them as final.

source: RBI Master Direction (Commercial Banks - Treatment of Wilful Defaulters and Large Defaulters) Directions, 2025, issued 28 November 2025; catalog PDF: rbidocs.rbi.org.in/rdocs/notification/PDFs/166MD.PDF (CAPTCHA-gated for direct fetch — content below is cross-checked from multiple regulatory-tracking sources reporting the official text; verify against the primary Direction before treating as legally binding)
text: RBI Master Direction — Treatment of Wilful Defaulters and Large Defaulters Purpose: a transparent, non-discriminatory framework for identifying wilful/large defaulters and sharing that information across the financial system, so other lenders don't unknowingly extend further credit to them. Wilful Defaulter — Definition: A borrower or guarantor who has committed "wilful default" AND whose outstanding amount is Rs. 25 lakh or above. Wilful default itself means: intentional/deliberate misuse, diversion, or siphoning of loan funds; failing to honour repayment despite having the capacity to pay; or breaching agreed loan covenants without justification. Consequences of Being Classified a Wilful Defaulter: - Barred from further credit from the banking system. - Restrictions on restructuring existing facilities or starting new ventures. - Reported to Credit Information Companies (monthly). - Details published (name disclosure). - Possible criminal proceedings, separate from the credit consequences. Preventive/Ongoing Obligations on Banks: - Proper credit appraisal before sanctioning. - End-use monitoring of disbursed funds (checking money is used for its stated purpose). - Involvement of statutory auditors or forensic auditors where diversion is suspected. - Monthly reporting of large and wilful defaulters to Credit Information Companies, with accurate reporting of any associated/ connected parties. Due Process: classification follows principles of natural justice (the borrower gets an opportunity to respond) before being formally declared a wilful defaulter — it is not an automatic/unilateral label.

text: RBI Regulated Entities — How To Verify a Financial Institution is Genuine RBI maintains a public directory/search tool letting anyone verify whether a financial institution is genuinely regulated by RBI, before depositing money or doing business with it — an important fraud- prevention check. Categories Searchable in RBI's Directory: - Scheduled Commercial Banks (SCBs) and their branches. - Non-Banking Finance Companies (NBFCs). - Foreign bank branches and representative offices operating in India. - Full-Fledged Money Changers and Authorised Dealers (forex). - Credit Information Companies. - Primary Dealers (government securities market). - Payment System Operators (payment gateways, wallets, etc.). - Mobile banking and prepaid payment instrument (PPI) issuers. - Banks authorised to import gold/silver. - Agency banks handling government business (tax collection, pension disbursement, etc.). Why This Matters: A common fraud pattern is an entity claiming RBI approval/registration it does not actually have (e.g. a fake NBFC or unauthorised digital lending app). Checking the entity's name against RBI's official list in the relevant category is the direct way to confirm genuine regulatory status before a customer commits funds — this is also relevant to RBI's Digital Lending Apps (DLA) list published separately by regulated entities, which serves the same verification purpose for lending apps specifically. This is a lookup tool, not a static list — the current, authoritative answer for any specific entity's status should always be checked live on RBI's site rather than assumed from memory.
